concept.technique_name: clue-driven blank matching in a three-blank text completion

examples.problem_statement: According to supporters of progressive taxation, the payment of higher tax rates by those with higher incomes, those who (i) _________ such taxation systems tend to fall into two camps: the (ii) _________, who feel it unjust that the “most industrious” among us are “penalized” for their success, and the (iii) _________, who argue that higher taxes on the rich will harm us all by dampening the entrepreneurial spirit that drives the economy. Blank (i): rail against / vote for / depredate. Blank (ii): autodidacts / moralists / recidivists. Blank (iii): libertines / utilitarians / myrmidons.

solution.operation: Read the definition of progressive taxation given in the sentence, then read how the two camps are described: they “feel it unjust” that the “most industrious” are “penalized”
solution.result: The people named in blank (i) are definitely against progressive taxation
solution.description: Take the sentence's own description of the two camps as the clue that fixes the stance of the group in blank (i) before looking at any answer choice.

solution.operation: Test the blank (i) choices against the meaning “be against”: rail against, vote for, depredate
solution.description: Pick the blank (i) word that expresses opposition; the sentence's clue about feeling penalized rules out an approving word.

solution.operation: Match blank (ii) to the clue word “unjust”, and check the rejects: autodidacts are people who teach themselves, recidivists are people who return to committing crimes
solution.description: Use the justice language in the clause attached to blank (ii) to select the group defined by a moral objection, discarding the two words whose definitions have nothing to do with the sentence.

solution.operation: For blank (iii), find a second opposed group that differs from the moralists because it makes a practical argument — higher taxes harm us all by dampening the entrepreneurial spirit
solution.description: Select the blank (iii) word for people who judge by practical consequences rather than by justice, which is what distinguishes this camp from the one in blank (ii).

key_reminders: The clause attached to each blank supplies the clue for that blank; read it before the choices.
The second and third camps must both oppose progressive taxation yet differ in kind — moral objection versus practical objection.
A choice whose dictionary definition is irrelevant to the sentence is wrong no matter how hard the word is.
common_mistakes: Choosing “vote for” in blank (i) by reading the sentence as describing supporters of progressive taxation rather than the camps that object to it.
Picking “autodidacts” or “recidivists” for blank (ii) on the strength of difficulty alone, when neither definition connects to the word “unjust”.
Filling blank (iii) with another moral-sounding word instead of one that captures a practical, consequence-based argument.

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for the blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill the blank in the way that best completes the text. Even as the economy struggled, the secretary stood by his ______ long-term outlook, saying that technology was allowing businesses to make deep-rooted improvements in their productivity, the best indicator of an economy’s ability to grow. (A) arcane (B) sanguine (C) equivocal (D) ambivalent (E) irresolute

solution.operation: Set the current struggles of the economy against the secretary's predictions for its long-term prospects, as the word “Even” signals
solution.result: The blank must describe an outlook that runs counter to the present struggle
solution.description: Read the concessive opening as a contrast so the blank is anchored to the secretary's long-term view rather than to the economy's current state.

solution.operation: Read what the secretary says: technology is allowing deep-rooted productivity improvements, the best indicator of an economy's ability to grow
solution.result: The secretary believes technology will lead to economic growth, so his outlook is optimistic
solution.description: Use the second half of the sentence, which states the secretary's reasoning, to name the outlook precisely: optimistic.

solution.result: Choices C, D, E are out
solution.description: Discard the three words that imply wavering or openness to alternate interpretations, since nothing in the sentence indicates the secretary's view has wavered.
Drop the remaining wrong choice because the sentence explains the rationale for the outlook straightforwardly, so the outlook is not an obscure one.

solution.operation: Match the surviving choice to “optimistic”: sanguine
solution.description: Confirm that the one word left carries the meaning the clue demanded, which makes it the answer.

key_reminders: “Even as” marks a contrast: the blank opposes the struggling economy, not matches it.
The stated rationale in the second half of the sentence defines the blank; predict the meaning before reading the choices.
common_mistakes: Treating the struggling economy as the clue and choosing a doubt word such as equivocal, ambivalent, or irresolute.
Choosing arcane because the sentence sounds technical, even though its explanation of the outlook is plainly given.

concept.technique_name: drawing radii to form right triangles and applying the Pythagorean theorem
concept.sub_category: circles and right triangles in quantitative comparison

examples.problem_statement: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B. O is the center of the circle above, and x is the length of a line segment drawn from O to a point inside the circle (the figure supplies a right triangle with legs of length 3 and 4). Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 5. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.operation: State the comparison: x is the length of a line segment from the center of the circle to a point inside the circle, to be compared with 5
solution.description: Fix what x actually measures in the figure before doing any computation, since it is a segment from the center to an interior point.

solution.operation: Draw two radii in the figure, each one completing a right triangle
solution.result: Two right triangles, one of them with both legs known
solution.description: Add the easiest segments to work with in a circle — the radii — so that the figure yields right triangles you can compute with.

solution.operation: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the triangle whose legs have lengths 3 and 4 and whose hypotenuse is the radius r: r^2 = 3^2 + 4^2
solution.description: Use the triangle in which both leg lengths are known to set up an equation for the radius.

solution.operation: Take the positive square root: r = \sqrt{25}
solution.description: Solve for the radius, keeping only the positive root because a length cannot be negative.

solution.operation: Compare the segment of length x with the radius, since x is clearly shorter than the radius in the figure
solution.description: Read the size relation off the figure now that the radius has a number attached, which settles the comparison.

solution.operation: Alternatively, observe that the two right triangles are congruent, so x equals the leg of length 4
solution.description: Confirm the same conclusion by the congruence route, which pins x to an exact value instead of only bounding it.

examples.answer: Choice B: Quantity B is greater.

key_reminders: In a circle, the radius and the diameter are the easiest segments to work with; drawing radii often creates usable right triangles.
Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs.
Any segment from the center to a point strictly inside the circle is shorter than the radius.
common_mistakes: Comparing x with the leg lengths 3 and 4 instead of first computing that the radius is 5.
Assuming the relationship cannot be determined because x is not labeled with a number, when the 3-4 triangle determines the radius.
Concluding the quantities are equal by mistaking x for the radius rather than for a shorter interior segment.
